name: CN I Olfactory nerve
modality: Special sensory: olfaction; often classified as special visceral afferent in traditional cranial-nerve schemes
course: Receptor-neuron axon bundles pass through cribriform foramina to the olfactory bulb in the anterior cranial fossa. The bulb and tract are CNS structures along the orbital frontal surface; their axons continue through olfactory striae to central olfactory targets. The depicted course is schematic and does not resolve individual fila.
function: CN I consists of primary olfactory receptor-neuron axons (olfactory fila) from the superior nasal neuroepithelium to the bulb. Mitral/tufted cells then project in the CNS olfactory tract to primary olfactory regions without a compulsory initial thalamic relay. Olfaction contributes to flavor and emotional/memory networks, but it is distinct from gustatory taste.

afferent: Bipolar olfactory receptor neurons in the superior nasal neuroepithelium
efferent: First synapse in olfactory-bulb glomeruli on mitral/tufted cells
Bulb output continues in olfactory tract to piriform/periamygdaloid and other olfactory regions; higher processing includes orbitofrontal/MD pathways

bloodSupply: Nasal mucosa is supplied by ethmoidal and other nasal arteries; bulb/tract receive small ACA/carotid-system branches. Segment-specific territory is not mapped here.

clinical.findings: May follow nasal obstruction/inflammation, viral injury, trauma, intracranial disease or neurodegeneration; reduced smell alone does not establish one neurological diagnosis.
Shearing of fila at the cribriform plate or injury of bulb/tract can impair smell; degree of recovery varies.
A large anterior cranial-fossa lesion can cause ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema, sometimes with anosmia; the full pattern is uncommon.

name: CN II Optic nerve
modality: Special somatic afferent: vision/reflex retinal output from the ipsilateral eye before partial chiasmal crossing
course: From optic disc through intraorbital and canalicular segments, the nerve passes the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery, then continues in the suprasellar region to the chiasm. Posterior nerve is oligodendrocyte-myelinated and surrounded by meninges with a continuous subarachnoid sheath. The displayed course does not establish patient-specific canal or orbital anatomy.
function: CN II conveys retinal ganglion-cell output from one eye through the optic canal to the chiasm. The optic nerve is a CNS tract by development and myelination, conventionally named a cranial nerve. Its retinal axons contribute to visual, pupillary and circadian pathways after their central continuation.

afferent: Retinal ganglion-cell axons from the ipsilateral eye; retinal circuitry has already processed the input
efferent: Continuation through chiasm into optic tracts
Retinal axons ultimately reach LGN, pretectal, collicular and hypothalamic targets; these are not separate synapses within the nerve

bloodSupply: Optic-nerve head: mainly short posterior ciliary branches; orbital/canalicular nerve: ophthalmic/pial circulation; intracranial nerve: small carotid/ACA-related branches. Central retinal artery principally supplies inner retina.

clinical.findings: Inflammatory, ischemic, compressive or traumatic injury can cause monocular visual loss, color/field abnormalities and asymmetric afferent pupillary responses; prognosis and pain vary.
Raised intracranial pressure can produce optic-disc swelling through the meningeal sheath; not every swollen disc is papilledema.
Central retinal artery occlusion primarily injures inner retina; posterior ciliary ischemia can injure optic-nerve head. These are distinct anterior visual-pathway sites.
